description: Everything on raskell.io as one index: articles, reviews, notes, talks, works from the reading log, projects, topics, and every external link the writing cites. The same index the site's search uses.

items.title: Shiioo, Re-imagined, and the Home AI Lab It Runs On
items.description: How I re-imagined Shiioo with what 2026 taught me about agent systems, and why my local setup moves to a Mac Studio and DGX Sparks.

items.title: Win Everything, Control No One
items.description: Sebastian Mallaby's biography of Demis Hassabis is the best history of modern AI I know, and an honest study of a man who hates control and exercises it.

items.title: After PHP Gate: A Blueprint for the Static Web
items.description: Last week's PHP flaws reached every server that runs code per request. My blueprint for sites and apps that run none at all.

items.title: Learning to Play
items.description: A chess prodigy's handbook, three old games and one laptop: rebuilding the ideas behind game-playing AI in Rust for a browser on my phone, and measuring them.

items.title: The Web Was the Training Set
items.description: Tim Berners-Lee's memoir is the story of a British engineer at a Franco-Swiss lab giving a protocol away. Read in 2026, it is also the origin story of AI's data supply.

items.title: Observability Is Not Logging
items.description: A cost total says nothing about how a run went. This part turns each agent run into a trace: which turn escalated, which tool failed, where the money went.

items.title: This Site Is Becoming a Map
items.description: A blog shows what I wrote last. The new map on raskell.io shows what I keep coming back to, and it is the start of a public second brain.

items.title: The Bill Is Part of the Loop
items.description: Every model response already carries its own bill in the usage field, and the loop throws it away. This post reads that field, prices it against a table, and turns cost into a value the loop can see per turn and act on: a metering decorator that needs no loop change, a running ledger, prompt-cache accounting that moves the number the most, and a budget that degrades before it stops. Part eight of The Agent Platform Handbook.

items.title: The Model Is a Dependency
items.description: Every layer of the harness has existed to put the right tokens in front of one hardcoded model string. This post pulls that string out and makes the model a dependency: why you route a cheap model for easy turns and a strong one for hard turns, what a fallback looks like when a provider is down, and why 'models are commodities' is a claim about your architecture before it is a claim about the market. Part seven of The Agent Platform Handbook.

items.title: The Bottleneck Is Data, and Europe Is Sitting on It
items.description: Frontier AI is running short on public text, not compute. Europe's edge is the high-quality data it never put online. Capturing it needs coordination.

items.title: Brain Emulation, Read as an Infrastructure Problem
items.description: An MIT thesis argues brain emulation has crossed into engineering. Read as infrastructure, the numbers describe a workload your AI cluster was not built for.

items.title: Memory Is a Write Path
items.description: Retrieval reads context the project authored. Memory is the agent writing context for its own future sessions, and the write is the part that is dangerous. Why session memory comes free from the transcript, why cross-session memory needs a separate write surface, and how to let an agent remember without letting it corrupt its own ground truth. Part six of The Agent Platform Handbook.

items.title: The Proof You Only Have to Write Once
items.description: Generation is cheap, so verification is the bottleneck — and we throw the verification away every time. What if a proof, once written, could be named, shared, and vouched for? A content-addressed commons for verified Haskell, and the move I left for after the semantic-artifact trilogy.

items.title: Retrieval Is a Tool, Not a Layer
items.description: Loading the whole .AGENTS/ directory on every turn does not scale. The fix is not a retrieval layer bolted to the side of the agent. It is a search tool in the registry the agent already has. BM25 over project docs, no vector store, and an honest account of when embeddings start to earn their keep. Part five of The Agent Platform Handbook.

items.title: Context Is the Product
items.description: Models are commodities. Context is not. The sources of context an agent draws on, why retrieval alone is not enough, and a minimal .AGENTS/ convention that loads context from disk into the same harness we have been building. Part four of The Agent Platform Handbook.

items.title: Tools: How Agents Actually Do Things
items.description: Function calling is the API between language and action, but the engineering is in the registry. A working four-tool registry in TypeScript on Bun, schema design that survives model drift, parallel tool calls, and the failure modes nobody mentions in the demo. Part three of The Agent Platform Handbook.

items.title: Your Agent Wants Root
items.description: An agent with a shell tool is arbitrary code execution with a friendly face. A short tour of why Docker alone is not enough, what Firecracker, gVisor, and Kata actually solve, and a hardened sandbox you can wrap the post-one agent in today. Part two of The Agent Platform Handbook.

items.title: What an Agent Actually Is
items.description: AI agent is the most overloaded word in the industry. This is the anatomy, the lineage, and a working implementation in roughly two hundred lines of TypeScript on Bun. Part one of The Agent Platform Handbook.

items.title: The Field Exists Now
items.description: Alasdair Allan's agentlanguages.dev catalogue turns AI-oriented programming languages from a loose set of experiments into a field with camps, disagreements, and testable claims.

items.title: Source Code Is the New Assembly

items.description: Human continuity platform for preserving presence across generations. Humankind helps people build a living archive of voice, stories, memories, values, and relational warmth so the texture of a person remains accessible long after distance, aging, or death would otherwise erase it. Consent-first, privacy by default, and explicit about the difference between recorded truth, reconstruction, and inference.

items.title: Arcanist
items.description: Haskell tooling for the age of AI-authored code. hx is a fast package and project manager written in Rust, and bhc is a compiler built to check everything it can. With a registry that records what has been verified, they lead toward a commons where nobody, human or model, has to verify the same thing twice.

items.title: Zentinel
items.description: Security-first reverse proxy built to guard the free web. Rust on Cloudflare's Pingora, explicit configuration over hidden defaults, and WAF, auth and other policy in isolated agents, so a crashing agent leaves the proxy running. Agents for WAF, bot management, identity, API inspection and scripting, SDKs from Rust to Haskell, a pure Rust ModSecurity engine and a fleet control plane.

items.title: hx
items.description: The Haskell toolchain in one fast binary. hx installs GHC and Cabal, builds, tests, formats and lints your code, pins every dependency by hash, and publishes your packages. Written in Rust, it starts in milliseconds, works with the .cabal files and Hackage you already use, and gives AI agents the same commands over MCP.

items.title: bhc
items.description: The Basel Haskell Compiler, a clean-slate compiler for the Haskell you already write. Written in Rust, it compiles to native code through LLVM and to WebAssembly, with a runtime profile chosen per build. It compiles all 221 modules of Pandoc, and Pandoc's Markdown reader and HTML writer run end to end.

items.title: Shiioo
items.description: A virtual company of AI agents on your Mac, run from your phone. Claude Code, Codex and local models work in their own branches; a rules file decides what they may do alone, the rest reaches you on Telegram as a question, and every step lands in a tamper-evident record. One Rust binary, open source.

items.title: Refrakt
items.description: A convention-first web framework for Gleam. Productive like Phoenix, explicit like Gleam, composable with Wisp and Lustre. Full-stack code generation, CRUD scaffolding, and a batteries-included developer experience on the BEAM.

items.title: Vela
items.description: No-downtime app deployment on bare metal. One binary. No containers. A self-hosted PaaS alternative to Heroku, Fly.io, Coolify, and Kamal. Built in Rust with zero-downtime deploys and a built-in reverse proxy.

items.title: broodwar.live
items.description: The community platform for StarCraft: Brood War competitive play, a basketball-reference.com for Brood War. Profiles for 150 pro players in English and Korean, build orders for every matchup, tournaments, a wiki, and replay analysis that runs in the browser on WebAssembly, so nothing is uploaded.

items.title: Die Zukunft
items.description: A Swiss movement that applies engineering principles to public life: not left, not right. Digital sovereignty through open standards, auditable and portable public infrastructure, and policy grounded in evidence, with its own research pipeline for Swiss federal data.

items.title: Human Macroscope
items.description: A long-term interdisciplinary research project on humans and human collectives across scales, from individuals and families to institutions, cultures, and civilizations: how individual traits, roles, relations, and cultural transmission combine into emergent collective properties.

items.title: Chronicle of Earth
items.description: An interactive atlas of history and geopolitics, starting with 1900–2026. An early prototype pairs a 3D globe that zooms down to villages and streets with a timeline spanning days to decades. Its data model keeps events, territorial claims, control, sources, and uncertainty distinct. Historical coverage is still a small draft collection; detailed base maps show present-day geography.

items.title: WASM-AD
items.description: A fantasy console standard with 32-bit handheld hardware: tile layers, sprites, palettes, and save RAM, memory-mapped inside the cartridge. A cartridge is a single WebAssembly module. Comes with a written spec, a reference renderer with conformance tests, SDKs for Rust, C and C++, Zig, AssemblyScript and Go, and a web player.

items.title: coconutOS
items.description: A hard shell for AI inference. A Rust microkernel that makes GPU isolation a kernel primitive: every model runs in its own shard with its own page tables, VRAM partition and capabilities, GPU drivers live outside ring 0, and pledge_gpu and unveil_vram only ever take privileges away. Runs a transformer forward pass end to end in QEMU today; real GPU silicon is next.

items.title: Terrarium
items.description: A societal simulation engine where LLM-powered agents form emergent civilizations. Each agent has a personality, needs, memories, and beliefs that can be wrong. You set the rules of the world, then watch for markets, hierarchies, and alliances to emerge on their own.

items.title: Hotaru
items.description: Simulated neuron cultures on a 60-electrode array play Pong in your browser, as in the DishBrain experiment. Feedback for hits and misses alone did not make them better. Input that goes quiet when the paddle moves toward the ball did, and the page shows it next to a control.

items.title: Kishi
items.description: Chess, shogi and Go against engines written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly. They play in the browser on your own device, offline, from novice to full strength, on a quiet board.

items.title: Sango
items.description: Edge diagnostics for the modern web. An operator-grade CLI that performs comprehensive endpoint analysis in a single command. TLS inspection, HTTP protocol detection (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3), security headers, latency measurements, and technology stack identification.

items.title: Conflux
items.description: Schema-aware config state coordination. Multiple writers, deterministic merge, git milestones. A CRDT document engine with pluggable storage backends (SQLite, PostgreSQL, DynamoDB).

items.title: Ushio
items.description: Deterministic edge traffic replay for understanding WAF and proxy behavior. Capture traffic as HAR files, rewrite URLs for staging/production comparison, mutate headers, strip cookies, and diff WAF responses across environments.

items.title: Driftscape
items.description: Ambient soundscape platform. composable, location-aware, AI-powered background music.

items.title: robogym
items.description: Rust/Bevy PWA for training robotic agents. Democratizing robotics through browser-based simulation.

items.title: Awesomeify
items.description: Index GitHub repos and generate static awesome-list sites.

items.title: Learn You the Web
items.description: A friendly guide to how the web actually works. For Real This Time. HTTP, DNS, TLS, and the protocols that hold it all together. without the hand-waving or oversimplification.

items.title: Manabi
items.description: A reading-first language-learning app for Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Hebrew. It trains recognition, pronunciation, listening, context, and recall separately, with spaced repetition and prerecorded native audio. It runs offline in the browser and installs as a PWA.

items.title: Kurumi
items.description: A local-first, AI-native second brain. Capture notes, links, and meetings, then find them again through wikilinks, backlinks, a graph view, and full-text search. Everything works offline, with optional sync through Automerge CRDTs and no vendor lock-in.

items.title: Paw & Claw
items.description: A turn-based strategy game in the spirit of Advance Wars, fought by woodland armies. Raccoons, badgers, lions, red pandas, and moles fight over every thicket and creek. Built in Rust with Bevy. Play it free in the browser, or as a desktop build.

items.title: Rainbow River
items.description: A fishing game in the style of the 32-bit handhelds, inspired by The Legend of the River King. Walk the river, read the water, and fill a fish log of hand-drawn species. Written in Rust, compiled to WebAssembly, and the first cartridge for WASM-AD. It plays in the browser.

items.title: Abstraction
items.description: Layers that let people stop thinking about the layer below, from assembly and programming languages to orchestrators and agents, and how each new layer becomes the ground for the next.

items.title: Agent identity
items.description: Agents as principals of their own: identities, entitlements, credentials, budgets and audit trails provisioned like an employee's, with a human sponsor, instead of borrowed rights.

items.title: Agents
items.description: LLM agents as software: the loop, tools, context, memory, sandboxes, and the platform underneath them.

items.title: AI alignment
items.description: Making AI systems pursue what their builders and users actually intend, and what happens when they do not.

items.title: AI-assisted engineering
items.description: AI as an engineering tool: coding agents, AI-authored code, and what programming becomes when models write most of it.

items.title: AI for operations
items.description: AI applied to running systems: security triage, alert noise, incident work, and keeping a human in the loop.

items.title: AI platforms
items.description: The shared foundation an organisation builds AI on: model gateways, agent runtimes, governance, observability, and the operating model around them.

items.title: Applied security
items.description: Security under production pressure: adversarial input, signal versus noise, and controls that operators can live with.

items.title: Attention economy
items.description: Platforms that sell attention and optimise for engagement, what that does to the web and to discourse, and the intention economy proposed in its place.

items.title: Augmentation
items.description: Computers that extend what people can do instead of replacing them: Licklider's symbiosis, Kasparov's centaur chess, and working alongside coding agents.

items.title: Cities
items.description: How cities are planned and how they actually grow: Jerusalem over three thousand years, Brasilia drawn on paper, and the rational city the web was designed against.

items.title: The commons
items.description: Resources held in common and the rules that keep them so: common land, open protocols, open data, and the web before the platforms.

items.title: Compilers
items.description: Turning programs into other programs: parsers, interpreters, type checkers, and code generation.

items.title: Complex systems
items.description: Emergence and collective dynamics: how simple agents, roles, and rules add up to markets, institutions, and societies.

items.title: Context engineering
items.description: Deciding what a model sees: pinned context, retrieval, memory, and the conventions that keep them honest.

items.title: Cryptocurrency
items.description: Bitcoin, blockchains and distributed ledgers: the attempt to formalise money and trust so completely that no institution is needed, and the institutions that grew back around it.

items.title: Data sovereignty
items.description: Control over one's own data: pods, portability, and the right to choose the software and the agent that reads it; the personal counterpart of national sovereignty.

items.title: Decentralisation
items.description: Many small nodes and no central operator: the web's original shape, and the alternative to platforms that own the users and the data.

items.title: Democratisation
items.description: A capability that needed money, a team, or years of training becoming available to anyone: printing, the web, and now building software by describing it.

items.title: Determinism
items.description: Machines and institutions that do the same thing every time, what that sameness is worth, and where it breaks against an open world.

items.title: Developer tooling
items.description: Package managers, build tools, CLIs, and the daily toolchain an engineer actually touches.

items.title: Distributed systems
items.description: Replication, coordination, and consistency across machines that fail independently.

items.title: Durable execution
items.description: Workflow engines that keep long-running processes alive through crashes and deployments, with a journal of every step: Temporal, Restate and their kin.

items.title: Economics
items.description: Cost, pricing, budgets, and the money side of infrastructure, inference, and innovation.

items.title: Edge systems
items.description: Reverse proxies, policy enforcement, CDNs, and logic that runs close to the user instead of in the backend.

items.title: Elixir
items.description: Elixir, Phoenix, and the BEAM for the long-running, fault-tolerant parts.

items.title: Emergence
items.description: Order nobody designed: reefs, the early web, neuron cultures, and simulated worlds where simple rules add up to behaviour no single part has.

items.title: Enterprise architecture
items.description: How a company's capabilities, applications, data and infrastructure fit together, who owns what, and how the landscape is changed on purpose.

items.title: Entrepreneurship
items.description: Finding something worth building and building it: ventures, side projects, and what changes when anyone can spot an opportunity and operate a business with AI.

items.title: Ethics
items.description: Right and wrong under pressure: guilt and freedom in novels, the responsibility of scientists, and what we owe the systems we build and the people they affect.

items.title: Europe
items.description: Europe's place in technology and history: where the web was invented, what it builds and gives away, and the data and capabilities it still holds.

items.title: Evaluation
items.description: Measuring whether an AI system does the right thing: golden sets, structural checks, LLM-as-judge, and regression suites.

items.title: Existential risk
items.description: Technologies that could end or permanently cripple civilisation, from nuclear weapons to misaligned AI, and how people have tried to contain them.

items.title: External memory
items.description: Notes, links, and stores that remember for us: second brains, the web as a shared memory, and what agents write down for their next session.

items.title: Factories
items.description: Machines that make machines: the factory pattern in code, real plants, universal constructors, and purpose-built things made on demand.

items.title: Finance
items.description: Banks, insurers, money and credit: abstract businesses that sell kept promises, allocate a society's resources and turn trust into procedure.

items.title: Formal methods
items.description: Proofs, verification, and types as specifications, especially once machines write the code.

items.title: Fractals
items.description: Self-similar patterns that repeat at every scale, from rivers and coastlines to software, organisations and ideas; the lens behind much of this site.

items.title: Future of work
items.description: What AI does to jobs and livelihoods: the interval before any post-scarcity economy, basic income against basic access, and who gets through the middle.

items.title: Game AI
items.description: Programs that play games: search, evaluation, learned networks, and how their strength is measured, from chess engines to Go and real-time strategy.

items.title: Games
items.description: Games made with care: tactics, fishing, and the engines and fantasy consoles they run on.

items.title: Geography
items.description: Places, terrain, borders, and spatial data, and how their relationships change over time.

items.title: Geopolitics
items.description: How geography, empires, and arms shape the balance of power between states and regions, as history.

items.title: GPUs
items.description: GPUs as the computer: memory shape, partitioning, and the hardware under inference.

items.title: Haskell
items.description: The language that shaped how I think about types, effects, and correctness.

items.title: High modernism
items.description: The confidence that society can be planned from above by experts: Le Corbusier's rational city, scientific forestry, and the schemes that failed when they met real life.

items.title: History
items.description: Events, institutions, and societies through time, with attention to sources, competing accounts, and uncertainty.

items.title: History of science
items.description: How discoveries were actually made: the people, instruments, dead ends, and institutions behind them.

items.title: History of technology
items.description: How tools, machines, and networks came to be built, and the choices that shaped them.

items.title: Hubris
items.description: When builders overestimate their control: an island of cloned dinosaurs, cities planned on paper, the bomb, and systems more capable than their makers understand.

items.title: Hypertext
items.description: Links as the unit of the web: addresses that can point at anything, the read-write web that was intended, and what a graph of documents can do that a tree cannot.

items.title: Inference
items.description: Running models in production: routing, cost, hardware, and inference as a metered utility.

items.title: Insurance
items.description: Pooling risk across many so that misfortune does not ruin the few: predictions wrapped in promises, from Halley's life table to cars that price their own drivers.

items.title: Intellectual property
items.description: Patents, copyright, and licences: who owns an invention or a text, from the web given to the public domain to books scraped for training data.

items.title: Intelligence
items.description: What intelligence is and how it arises, in brains, in neuron cultures, and in machines that learn.

items.title: Isolation
items.description: Sandboxes, process and failure-domain isolation, and running untrusted or fallible work safely.

items.title: Knowledge management
items.description: Second brains, knowledge graphs, and how notes, links, and memory turn into understanding.

items.title: Kubernetes
items.description: Container orchestration, and the question of when you actually need it.

items.title: Languages and translation
items.description: Human languages and moving meaning between them: translated novels, learning to read Chinese, Japanese, and Hebrew, and Europe's multilingual text.

items.title: Legibility
items.description: Making a complex system readable from above: what the measure captures, what it erases, and what breaks when the map replaces the territory.

items.title: Life sciences
items.description: Biology and medicine: how living systems work, and how we learn to measure, model, and treat them.

items.title: Linux
items.description: Linux distributions and system administration, Void Linux in particular.

items.title: Literature
items.description: Fiction and writing about fiction: novels read for their own sake, and the forms they take.

items.title: Local-first
items.description: Software that keeps data on your devices and syncs through CRDTs, with the network as an optimisation.

items.title: Machine learning
items.description: How models learn from data: the mathematics, the training methods, and what the results can and cannot do.

items.title: Mathematics
items.description: The mathematics underneath the systems on this site: probability, linear algebra, optimisation, and proof.

items.title: Maximalist novels
items.description: Very long, encyclopedic novels that try to hold a whole world: Infinite Jest, The Books of Jacob, and the studies of the form.

items.title: Medicine
items.description: How treatments are discovered, tested, and brought to patients, from antisepsis and sulfa drugs to modern drug design.

items.title: This site
items.description: Posts about raskell.io itself: why it exists, how it is built, and where it is going.

items.title: Metrics
items.description: What to measure, leading versus lagging signals, and vanity numbers that look like insight.

items.title: Networking
items.description: How machines talk: packets, protocols, sockets, and the networks from ARPANET to the web that carry them.

items.title: Neural networks
items.description: Layers of weights that learn a function from examples: architectures, activations, quantisation, and running them where the data is.

items.title: Neuroscience
items.description: Brains and nervous systems: connectomes, neural recording, and the attempt to model what neurons compute.

items.title: Observability
items.description: Seeing what a running system does: traces, metering, glass-box infrastructure, and what not to log.

items.title: Open data
items.description: Data published for anyone to use: government records, archives, and the five-star ladder from a file on the web to linked data with addresses.

items.title: Open standards
items.description: Protocols and formats agreed in the open and free to implement: HTTP, HTML, TCP/IP, RSS, and the consortia and working groups that keep them so.

items.title: The open web
items.description: The web as a commons: open protocols, small independent sites, and publishing outside the platforms.

items.title: OpenBSD
items.description: OpenBSD and the BSD approach to correctness and simplicity.

items.title: OpenTelemetry
items.description: The vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics, and logs, including the GenAI semantic conventions for model calls.

items.title: Operating systems
items.description: Kernels, virtualisation, and the layer between hardware and everything else, from BSD to inference-native designs.

items.title: Open source
items.description: Open source as the point of the work, not just its licence.

items.title: Philosophy
items.description: Questions about knowledge, mind, morality, and belief, from how science knows things to the novels that argue with God.

items.title: Philosophy of science
items.description: How science produces knowledge, what counts as evidence, and where its methods and claims reach their limits.

items.title: Pingora
items.description: Cloudflare's Rust framework for building proxies, the base of Zentinel.

items.title: Platform automation
items.description: Self-service, guardrails, deployment, and the tooling that keeps operating software sustainable.

items.title: Policy
items.description: Where engineering meets regulation, public institutions, procurement, and national strategy.

items.title: Post-scarcity
items.description: What changes when making things costs next to nothing: copied software, AI labour, mission-built machines, and the economies and societies that might follow.

items.title: Privacy
items.description: Tracking, profiling, and consent on the web, and designs that avoid collecting the data in the first place.

items.title: Programming languages
items.description: Languages, type systems, compilers, and how executable intent gets written down.

items.title: Provenance
items.description: Where something came from and who vouches for it: signed media, rights-clear training data, and artifacts that carry their own history.

items.title: Reinforcement learning
items.description: Learning from the outcomes of one's own actions: self-play, rewards, and feedback loops that turn experience into skill.

items.title: Reliability
items.description: Failure modes, operability, and keeping systems up when the inputs and the dependencies misbehave.

items.title: Religion
items.description: Faith, doubt, and the institutions and cities built around belief, as history and as argument.

items.title: Research labs
items.description: The institutions where discovery happens and how they are funded and run: CERN, Bell Labs, ARPA, Los Alamos, DeepMind, and the labs behind modern medicine.

items.title: Risk
items.description: Uncertainty, fragility, and systems that fail in ways nobody planned for, from markets to theme parks to production.

items.title: Rust
items.description: The systems language most of the projects here are written in.

items.title: Science fiction
items.description: Fiction as a thought experiment: cloned dinosaurs and chaos theory, post-scarcity civilisations, singularities, and stories from the internet read in the same spirit.

items.title: Scientific revolutions
items.description: Moments when a field's picture of the world changes: the invention of modern science, molecular biology, antisepsis, and the first antibiotics.

items.title: Self-hosting
items.description: Running your own infrastructure, from a single bare-metal box to community-operated compute.

items.title: Self-play
items.description: A program improving by playing itself: generating its own training data, learning from the outcomes, and testing each generation against the last.

items.title: Simulation
items.description: Interactive worlds that mimic real ones: societies, economies, neuron cultures, and agents left to evolve on their own.

items.title: Social reform
items.description: Plans to redesign society or the economy, from nineteenth-century utopias to high-modernist states and basic income, and what happened when they met people.

items.title: Sovereignty
items.description: Who controls compute, data, and infrastructure, and in which jurisdiction; Europe's position in particular.

items.title: Switzerland
items.description: The country this site is written from: CERN in Geneva, Basel, Swiss innovation as measured and as lived, and Swiss civic projects.

items.title: Technology races
items.description: Powers racing to build a technology first, from the bomb and its deterrence to frontier AI and the data it needs.

items.title: Training data
items.description: What models learn from: web crawls, books, and licensed or unlicensed corpora; who holds what has not been scraped yet, and on what terms.

items.title: Tree search
items.description: Looking ahead by expanding a tree of moves: minimax and alpha-beta, Monte Carlo tree search, and the pruning and ordering that make them tractable.

items.title: Trust
items.description: Personal trust and system trust: why people rely on banks, procedures and software they cannot inspect, and how that reliance is earned.

items.title: TypeScript
items.description: TypeScript on Bun, the language of the Agent Platform Handbook code.

items.title: WAF and traffic inspection
items.description: Web application firewalls, rule tuning, traffic replay, and inspecting requests without drowning operators.

items.title: WebAssembly
items.description: Portable, sandboxed bytecode for running native-speed code in the browser and beyond.

items.title: World history
items.description: History told at the scale of continents and millennia: why societies diverged, and how the world came to look the way it does.

items.title: Zola
items.description: The static site generator this site and several project sites are built with.
